people.name: Paul of Tarsus
people.summary: A Pharisee from Tarsus who persecuted the early church until a vision of the risen Christ made him 'apostle to the Gentiles'. His missionary journeys planted churches across Asia Minor and Greece, and his letters — the earliest Christian writings — shaped all later theology of grace, faith, the Law and the church. Tradition holds he was beheaded in Rome under Nero.
keyIdeas: Justification by faith apart from works of the Law
Gentiles included in God's people without circumcision
The church as the body of Christ

people.name: Simon Peter
people.summary: A Galilean fisherman, leader of the Twelve and first preacher at Pentecost according to Acts. He led the Jerusalem community, accepted Gentiles at Cornelius's house and, by strong early tradition, was martyred in Rome under Nero. Catholics regard him as the first pope; others honour him as chief apostle without accepting papal claims derived from him.
keyIdeas: Leadership of the early Jerusalem church

people.name: James, brother of the Lord
people.summary: Called 'the brother of the Lord', James became leader of the Jerusalem church and presided at the council of Jerusalem. Known as 'the Just' for his Torah piety, he was stoned in 62 according to Josephus. The Letter of James is traditionally attributed to him.

people.name: John the Apostle
people.summary: Son of Zebedee and one of the inner circle of the Twelve. Tradition identifies him with the Beloved Disciple and the author of the Fourth Gospel, three letters and Revelation, and places his old age at Ephesus. Modern scholars debate these attributions.
keyIdeas: Eternal life now through knowing Christ

people.name: Thomas the Apostle
people.summary: One of the Twelve, remembered in John's Gospel for doubting and then confessing 'My Lord and my God'. Strong tradition, recorded in the Acts of Thomas and cherished by Kerala's Christians, holds that he evangelised Parthia and India, arriving in 52 and dying as a martyr at Mylapore around 72.

people.name: Clement of Rome
people.summary: Leader of the Roman church at the end of the first century, listed by Irenaeus as the third successor of Peter. His letter to the Corinthians (c. 96) urges order and humility and is the earliest Christian text outside the New Testament.

people.name: Ignatius of Antioch
people.summary: Bishop of Antioch who, under guard on his way to martyrdom in Rome, wrote seven letters to churches. He stressed the unity of the church around the bishop, the real flesh of Christ against docetism, and the Eucharist; he is the first to use the phrase 'catholic church'.

people.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
people.summary: Bishop of Smyrna who, according to Irenaeus, had known the apostle John. He wrote a letter to the Philippians and was burned at about 86 years old after refusing to curse Christ. The account of his death is the earliest martyr-act.

people.name: Justin Martyr
people.summary: Born in Samaria, Justin searched among the philosophical schools before conversion, then taught Christianity as the true philosophy in Rome. His Apologies and Dialogue with Trypho present Christ as the Logos who sowed seeds of truth among all peoples. He was beheaded around 165.

people.name: Marcion of Sinope
people.summary: A wealthy shipowner who taught in Rome that the God of Israel was a just but lesser creator distinct from the good Father revealed by Jesus. Excommunicated around 144, he founded churches with his own canon of edited Luke and Pauline letters, provoking the wider church to define its Scriptures.
keyIdeas: Two Gods: just creator and good Father

people.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
people.summary: Born in Smyrna, where as a youth he heard Polycarp, Irenaeus became bishop of Lyon after the persecution of 177. His Against Heresies refuted Valentinian Gnosticism by appeal to the apostolic rule of faith, the four Gospels and the succession of bishops, and his Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching summarises the faith. He taught that Christ 'recapitulates' humanity, reversing Adam's disobedience.
keyIdeas: Rule of faith and apostolic succession
Goodness of creation against Gnostic dualism

people.name: Montanus
people.summary: A recent convert in Phrygia (fl. c. 156–172) who, with the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, uttered ecstatic oracles as the mouthpiece of the Paraclete. The 'New Prophecy' urged strict fasting and readiness for martyrdom and expected the heavenly Jerusalem to descend at Pepouza.

people.name: Tertullian
people.summary: A brilliant and combative Carthaginian writer, the first major Christian author in Latin. He coined much of the West's Trinitarian vocabulary — trinitas, one substance in three persons — and wrote against Marcion and Praxeas; later in life he sympathised with the Montanist New Prophecy.

people.name: Vibia Perpetua
people.summary: A 22-year-old noblewoman and new mother of Carthage, martyred with her slave Felicity and fellow catechumens in the arena. Her prison diary, recording visions of a ladder to heaven and of combat with the devil, is among the earliest texts by a Christian woman.

people.name: Clement of Alexandria
people.summary: An Athenian-educated convert who led the catechetical school at Alexandria. In the Exhortation, Instructor and Miscellanies he presented Christ as the divine Teacher and Christianity as the fulfilment of Greek philosophy, describing the mature believer as the true 'gnostic'.
keyIdeas: Philosophy as preparation for the gospel

people.name: Origen
people.summary: The most prolific scholar of the early church, head of the Alexandrian school and later teacher at Caesarea. His Hexapla, commentaries and On First Principles pioneered textual criticism and spiritual exegesis. Tortured in the Decian persecution, he died soon after; some speculations (pre-existence of souls, universal restoration) were condemned in 553.

people.name: Cyprian of Carthage
people.summary: A wealthy rhetor converted in middle age who became bishop of Carthage. During the Decian persecution he led from hiding and then addressed the reconciliation of the lapsed; his treatise On the Unity of the Church taught that 'outside the church there is no salvation'. He was beheaded under Valerian.
keyIdeas: Unity of the church in the episcopate

people.name: Novatian
people.summary: A Roman presbyter and author of the first major Latin treatise On the Trinity. After Cornelius was elected bishop and favoured readmitting the lapsed, Novatian was consecrated rival bishop, founding a rigorist church that lasted for centuries. He may have died a martyr under Valerian.

people.name: Sabellius
people.summary: A third-century teacher in Rome (fl. c. 215) condemned by Pope Callistus. Little survives of his own words; opponents describe him as teaching that Father, Son and Spirit are successive modes or names of one divine person. 'Sabellianism' became the standard label for modalism.
keyIdeas: Modalism: one God revealed in three modes

people.name: Paul of Samosata
people.summary: Bishop of Antioch and an official of Queen Zenobia of Palmyra, deposed by a synod in 268 for teaching that Jesus was a man inspired by the divine Word rather than the Word incarnate. He is regarded as a representative of dynamic monarchianism or adoptionism.
keyIdeas: Rejection of a personal pre-existent Son

people.name: Antony of Egypt
people.summary: A Coptic Christian who, around 270, sold his inheritance on hearing Matthew 19:21 and withdrew into the desert, combating demons through prayer and fasting. Athanasius' Life of Antony made him the archetype of the desert hermit and the 'father of monks'.

place.name: Monastery of St Antony, Eastern Desert

people.name: Gregory the Illuminator
people.summary: Patron saint of Armenia, said to have been imprisoned in a pit at Khor Virap for some thirteen years before healing and converting King Tiridates III. Consecrated in Caesarea of Cappadocia, he became the first Catholicos of the Armenian church, around 301 (or c. 314).
keyIdeas: Conversion of a nation through its king
Armenian church founded on apostolic and Cappadocian roots

people.name: Arius
people.summary: An ascetic Alexandrian presbyter who taught that the Son of God, though divine and before all ages, was created by the Father: 'there was when he was not'. Condemned at Nicaea in 325 and later partly rehabilitated, he died in Constantinople before his readmission to communion.
keyIdeas: The Son is the first and highest creature
Father alone is unbegotten true God

people.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
people.summary: Bishop of Caesarea, pupil of the Origenist Pamphilus, and 'father of church history'. His Ecclesiastical History preserves countless earlier sources; his Life of Constantine and panegyrics framed the Christian emperor as God's agent. He signed the Nicene Creed while uneasy about homoousios.

people.name: Constantine I
people.summary: Roman emperor who attributed his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) to the Christian God, ended persecution and lavished patronage on the church. He summoned the Council of Nicaea, founded Constantinople and was baptised on his deathbed. Eastern churches venerate him as 'equal to the apostles'; others see in him the beginning of Christendom's compromise with power.

people.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
people.summary: Bishop of Alexandria for 45 years, exiled five times, who championed the Nicene faith against Arianism. On the Incarnation argues that the Word became human so that humans might become divine; his Festal Letter of 367 is the first list of exactly the 27 New Testament books. He also wrote the Life of Antony.

people.name: Frumentius
people.summary: A Syrian-Greek youth shipwrecked and taken to the court of Aksum, where he rose to high office and supported Christian merchants. Consecrated bishop by Athanasius, he returned to evangelise the kingdom; Ethiopians honour him as Abba Salama, 'Father of Peace'.
keyIdeas: Ethiopian link to the see of Alexandria

people.name: Ezana of Aksum
people.summary: King of Aksum (reigned c. 320s–c. 360) who, tutored by Frumentius, became one of the first rulers anywhere to adopt Christianity. His inscriptions and coins move from pagan deities to 'the Lord of Heaven' and the cross.
keyIdeas: Royal adoption of Christianity in Africa

people.name: Nino of Georgia
people.summary: A woman from Cappadocia, remembered as a captive or pilgrim, whose healing prayers converted Queen Nana and King Mirian III of Kartli. Georgian Orthodoxy honours her as 'equal to the apostles' and enlightener of Georgia; her grapevine cross is a national symbol.

people.name: Ephrem the Syrian
people.summary: Deacon of Nisibis and later Edessa, the greatest poet-theologian of Syriac Christianity. His hundreds of madrashe (teaching hymns), sung by women's choirs, expressed doctrine through symbol and paradox rather than philosophy. He is honoured by every tradition and is a Doctor of the Catholic Church.
keyIdeas: Mary and the church in typology

people.name: Macrina the Younger
people.summary: Eldest sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who turned the family estate at Annisa into an ascetic community of women and men. Gregory's Life of Macrina and On the Soul and the Resurrection portray her as the family's spiritual teacher.

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.summary: Cappadocian theologian, called 'the Theologian' in the East, whose Five Theological Orations preached in Constantinople (380) defended the deity of Son and Spirit. Briefly archbishop and president of the council of 381, he resigned and retired to write poetry.
keyIdeas: Full deity of the Holy Spirit
What is not assumed is not healed

people.name: Basil of Caesarea
people.summary: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, called 'the Great', who shaped Eastern monastic life through his Rules and founded the Basileias, a complex of hospital and poor relief. His On the Holy Spirit defended the Spirit's equal glory and helped clarify one ousia in three hypostases.

people.name: Gregory of Nyssa
people.summary: The most philosophical of the Cappadocians, brother of Basil and Macrina. He developed the doctrine of the Trinity and of divine infinity, describing the spiritual life as endless progress (epektasis) into God; some of his writings hope for universal restoration.

people.name: Ambrose of Milan
people.summary: Roman governor acclaimed bishop of Milan while still unbaptised (374). He opposed Arian court influence, introduced antiphonal hymn-singing in the West, compelled Theodosius to do penance after the Thessalonica massacre and baptised Augustine in 387.

people.name: Jerome
people.summary: Dalmatian-born scholar, secretary to Pope Damasus, who settled in a monastery at Bethlehem with Paula and Eustochium. His Latin Vulgate translation, largely from the Hebrew, became the Western church's Bible; he was also a fierce controversialist.
keyIdeas: Hebraica veritas (priority of the Hebrew text)

people.name: John Chrysostom
people.summary: Preacher of Antioch nicknamed 'golden-mouthed', made archbishop of Constantinople in 398. His expository homilies on Scripture and denunciations of luxury and injustice made enemies at court; he died in exile. The most-used Orthodox liturgy bears his name. His sermons against Judaizing Christians contain harsh anti-Jewish rhetoric later misused.

people.name: Shenoute of Atripe
people.summary: Abbot of the White Monastery near Sohag for some eighty years, ruling thousands of monks and nuns. He is the greatest writer of Coptic literature; his zeal against pagan temples and for the poor, and his attendance at Ephesus (431) with Cyril, made him a hero of Coptic Christianity.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.summary: North African rhetor whose Confessions tell of his journey through Manichaeism and Neoplatonism to baptism by Ambrose in 387. As bishop of Hippo he wrote The City of God and On the Trinity and opposed Donatists and Pelagians. No theologian has shaped Western Christianity — Catholic and Protestant — more deeply.
keyIdeas: Church and sacraments valid apart from minister's holiness

people.name: Pelagius
people.summary: A British ascetic teacher in Rome who urged Christians to moral perfection, insisting that God commands nothing impossible. He and his followers denied that Adam's sin is inherited and that grace is needed to will the good; Augustine's opponents condemned his views in 416–418, though scholars debate how far he held the positions attributed to him.
keyIdeas: Human ability to obey God's commands

people.name: Mesrop Mashtots
people.summary: Armenian monk and scholar who created the Armenian alphabet around 405 and, with Catholicos Sahak, led the translation of the Bible and liturgy. He is also credited with alphabets for Georgian and Caucasian Albanian.

people.name: Cyril of Alexandria
people.summary: Patriarch of Alexandria who led the opposition to Nestorius and dominated the Council of Ephesus (431). He insisted on the single subject of the incarnate Word — 'one incarnate nature of God the Word' — and on Mary as Theotokos. Chalcedonians and Miaphysites both claim him as their authority; his episcopate was also marked by violent conflicts in Alexandria.
keyIdeas: One incarnate nature of the Word

people.name: Nestorius
people.summary: Antiochene monk made archbishop of Constantinople in 428, who objected to calling Mary Theotokos and preferred Christotokos to protect the distinct humanity of Christ. Deposed at Ephesus (431), he died in Egyptian exile; his Book of Heraclides denies teaching 'two sons'. The Church of the East venerates him as a saint and Greek Father.

people.name: Leo I (Leo the Great)
people.summary: Bishop of Rome from 440 whose Tome to Flavian, read at Chalcedon, taught that each nature in Christ acts in communion with the other. He articulated papal primacy as Peter speaking through his successor and reportedly persuaded Attila to withdraw from Italy (452).

people.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
people.summary: Cyril's successor as patriarch of Alexandria, who presided over the second Council of Ephesus (449). Deposed at Chalcedon in 451 — formally for disciplinary reasons — he died in exile at Gangra. The Coptic Orthodox Church honours him as a saint and confessor of Cyril's faith.
keyIdeas: Opposition to the Tome of Leo

people.name: Patrick
people.summary: A Romano-British deacon's son captured by Irish raiders at sixteen, who escaped and returned as a bishop to evangelise Ireland. His Confession and Letter to Coroticus reveal a humble, Bible-saturated faith and opposition to slavery. Dates are uncertain (traditionally 432–461).

people.name: Severus of Antioch
people.summary: Patriarch of Antioch (512–518) and the leading theologian of the anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) churches. Deposed by Justin I, he spent his last decades in Egypt. He argued against Eutyches that Christ is consubstantial with us, and against Chalcedon that 'in two natures' divides Christ.
keyIdeas: One composite nature of the incarnate Word
Rejection of Eutychianism and Chalcedon alike

people.name: Benedict of Nursia
people.summary: Italian hermit who founded monasteries at Subiaco and Monte Cassino and wrote the Rule of St Benedict — a 'little rule for beginners' balancing prayer (opus Dei), work and study under an abbot. Through Carolingian promotion it became the norm of Western monasticism; he is patron of Europe.

people.name: Jacob Baradaeus
people.summary: Syriac monk consecrated bishop of Edessa around 542 with Empress Theodora's support. Travelling in a ragged saddle-cloth disguise (hence 'Baradaeus'), he ordained dozens of bishops and thousands of clergy, establishing the Syriac Orthodox hierarchy.

people.name: Columba (Colum Cille)
people.summary: Irish monk of royal lineage who founded the monastery of Iona in 563, from which he and his monks evangelised the Picts. Adomnán's Life presents him as prophet and wonder-worker; Iona's mission later reached Northumbria.

people.name: Gregory the Great
people.summary: Roman prefect turned monk, elected pope in 590 amid plague and Lombard invasion. He organised relief, sent Augustine to England, wrote the Pastoral Rule and Moralia on Job, and called himself 'servant of the servants of God'. His theology transmitted Augustine to the medieval West.
keyIdeas: Purgatory and penance in popular teaching

people.name: Maximus the Confessor
people.summary: Byzantine monk and the great synthesiser of Greek patristic theology, who opposed imperial Monothelitism by insisting that Christ has a fully human will freely united with the divine. Tried in Constantinople, his tongue and right hand were cut off and he died in exile; the council of 681 vindicated him.

people.name: Isaac of Nineveh (Isaac the Syrian)
people.summary: Born in Beth Qatraye (Qatar), Isaac was briefly bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East before withdrawing to the mountains of Khuzistan. His ascetical homilies on humility, tears and God's boundless mercy were translated into Greek and became beloved across Orthodoxy despite his church affiliation.
keyIdeas: Mercy of God for all creation

people.name: Alopen
people.summary: A Church of the East missionary (fl. 635) from Persia or Syria, the first recorded Christian missionary to China. The Xi'an Stele says he arrived at Chang'an bearing scriptures and images and was welcomed by Emperor Taizong, who authorised a monastery in 638.
keyIdeas: Expression of the gospel in Chinese idiom

people.name: John of Damascus
people.summary: Born into a Christian family serving the Umayyad caliphs at Damascus, John became a monk at Mar Saba near Jerusalem. His Fount of Knowledge systematised Greek patristic doctrine, his Three Treatises defended icons on the basis of the incarnation, and he wrote one of the earliest Christian responses to Islam.

people.name: Timothy I
people.summary: Catholicos of the Church of the East (780–823) resident in Abbasid Baghdad. He debated Christianity respectfully with Caliph al-Mahdi, translated Aristotle for the caliph, and organised metropolitan provinces from Damascus to China and Tibet, presiding over the church's widest reach.

people.name: Charlemagne
people.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor from 800, Charlemagne united much of Western Europe, forcibly converted the Saxons and sponsored the Carolingian renaissance of learning, liturgy and script. His court promoted the Filioque and the Rule of Benedict.

people.name: Gottschalk of Orbais
people.summary: Saxon monk given to the monastery as a child, who taught a 'double predestination' of the elect to life and the reprobate to death, drawing on Augustine. Condemned at Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849), he spent the rest of his life imprisoned at Hautvillers.
keyIdeas: Christ died only for the elect

people.name: Photius I of Constantinople
people.summary: Immensely learned lay scholar elevated to patriarch in 858, whose dispute with Pope Nicholas I produced the 'Photian schism'. His Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit is the classic Orthodox case against the Filioque; he sent Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs. Orthodox venerate him as 'the Great'.
keyIdeas: Procession of the Spirit from the Father alone
Equality of patriarchates against papal jurisdiction

people.name: John Scotus Eriugena
people.summary: Irish scholar at the court of Charles the Bald who translated Pseudo-Dionysius and Maximus into Latin and wrote the Periphyseon, a Neoplatonic vision of all things proceeding from and returning to God. He opposed Gottschalk; some of his views were later condemned.
keyIdeas: Greek patristics in the Latin West

people.name: Cyril and Methodius
people.summary: Brothers from Thessalonica — Constantine-Cyril (c. 827–869) and Methodius (c. 815–885) — sent to Great Moravia in 863. They devised the Glagolitic alphabet and translated the Scriptures and liturgy into Slavonic, defending vernacular worship in Rome. Honoured as 'apostles to the Slavs' and patrons of Europe.

people.name: Symeon the New Theologian
people.summary: Abbot of St Mamas in Constantinople whose Hymns of Divine Love and Discourses describe visions of divine light and insist that conscious experience of the Holy Spirit is the birthright of every Christian. His teaching led to exile but foreshadowed hesychasm.

people.name: Vladimir the Great
people.summary: Grand Prince of Kyiv who, after a pagan youth, chose Byzantine Christianity around 988, married the emperor's sister Anna and ordered the baptism of his people. He built the Church of the Tithes and is venerated by Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians as baptiser of Rus'.
keyIdeas: Byzantine Orthodoxy among the East Slavs

people.name: Anselm of Canterbury
people.summary: Italian-born abbot of Bec and archbishop of Canterbury, a founder of scholasticism. His Proslogion offers the 'ontological argument' for God's existence ('that than which nothing greater can be conceived'), and Cur Deus Homo the satisfaction theory of atonement. He defended church liberty against English kings.

people.name: Peter Abelard
people.summary: Brilliant Paris master whose dialectical method (Sic et Non) and theology attracted crowds and controversy. After his love affair with Héloïse and castration, he became a monk; Bernard of Clairvaux secured his condemnation in 1141. He is associated with a 'moral influence' view of the atonement.

people.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
people.summary: Cistercian abbot and the dominant churchman of the twelfth century: mystic of the Song of Songs, adviser to popes, opponent of Abelard and preacher of the Second Crusade. Luther and Calvin admired his Christ-centred piety.

people.name: Hildegard of Bingen
people.summary: Benedictine abbess in the Rhineland whose visions, recorded in Scivias, were approved by Pope Eugenius III. She composed liturgical music, wrote on medicine and natural science, corresponded with emperors and popes and preached publicly. She was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

people.name: Joachim of Fiore
people.summary: Calabrian abbot who read history in three ages — of the Father, the Son and the Spirit — with a coming age of the Spirit and of contemplative monks. His Trinitarian criticism of Peter Lombard was condemned in 1215, but his apocalypticism inspired Spiritual Franciscans and later millennial thought.

people.name: Dominic de Guzmán
people.summary: Castilian canon who, after preaching to Cathars in Languedoc in poverty, founded the Order of Preachers (approved 1216) devoted to study and preaching. The Dominicans spread to universities across Europe; tradition credits him with promoting the rosary.

people.name: Francis of Assisi
people.summary: Son of a cloth merchant who renounced his wealth to live the Gospel in radical poverty, founding the Friars Minor and, with Clare, the Poor Clares. He met Sultan al-Kamil in Egypt (1219), composed the Canticle of the Creatures and reportedly received the stigmata in 1224.

people.name: Bonaventure
people.summary: Franciscan theologian at Paris and minister general of his order, often called its second founder. His Journey of the Mind into God unites Augustinian illumination with Franciscan devotion; he died during the Council of Lyon (1274).
keyIdeas: Ascent of the mind to God
Christ as centre of all knowledge

people.name: Thomas Aquinas
people.summary: Dominican friar and master at Paris, whose Summa Theologiae and Summa contra Gentiles integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Christian revelation. He taught that grace perfects nature, articulated transubstantiation and natural law, and offered the 'five ways' to God. Canonised in 1323, he became the Catholic Church's pre-eminent theologian.
keyIdeas: Transubstantiation explained through substance and accidents

people.name: John of Montecorvino
people.summary: Italian Franciscan who reached the Yuan capital Khanbaliq in 1294 after a stay in India, built churches, trained choirboys and translated the New Testament and Psalms. Named first archbishop of Khanbaliq (1307), he led the first Catholic mission in China until his death.

people.name: Rabban Sauma
people.summary: A Turkic (Önggüd or Uyghur) monk of the Church of the East born near Khanbaliq, who set out on pilgrimage to Jerusalem with his disciple Markos (later Catholicos Yahballaha III). Sent by the Ilkhan Arghun as ambassador to Europe in 1287, he met the Byzantine emperor, Pope Nicholas IV and the kings of France and England.
keyIdeas: Unity of Christians East and West

people.name: Meister Eckhart
people.summary: Dominican theologian and preacher whose German sermons speak of the birth of the Word in the soul and of detachment (Gelassenheit) leading into the 'ground' of God beyond all names. Some propositions were condemned in 1329, after his death; he remains a key figure of Western mysticism.
keyIdeas: Birth of God in the soul

people.name: John Duns Scotus
people.summary: Scottish Franciscan, the 'Subtle Doctor', who taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne. He argued for the univocity of being, the primacy of will and love, and the Immaculate Conception of Mary through 'preservative redemption' — a view defined as dogma in 1854.

people.name: William of Ockham
people.summary: English Franciscan whose nominalism denied the real existence of universals and stressed God's absolute power. Summoned to Avignon, he sided with the Franciscan Spirituals on poverty against John XXII and fled to the emperor in Munich. His 'razor' and covenantal theology influenced late medieval thought and young Luther's teachers.
keyIdeas: Absolute and ordained power of God

people.name: Gregory Palamas
people.summary: Athonite monk and archbishop of Thessalonica who defended hesychast prayer against Barlaam, distinguishing God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies in which believers truly participate. Councils of 1341–1351 upheld his teaching; he was canonised in 1368.

people.name: Sergius of Radonezh
people.summary: Hermit who founded the Holy Trinity monastery north-east of Moscow and introduced cenobitic life in Russia. Humble, peacemaking and revered as a wonderworker, he blessed Prince Dmitri before Kulikovo (1380) and inspired a wave of northern monastic foundations.

people.name: John Wycliffe
people.summary: Oxford philosopher and priest who argued that Scripture is the supreme authority, that the true church is the elect, and that a corrupt clergy forfeits its authority. He rejected transubstantiation and inspired the first complete English Bible. Condemned posthumously at Constance, he is called 'the Morning Star of the Reformation'.

people.name: Julian of Norwich
people.summary: English anchoress who, after sixteen visions during severe illness in 1373, wrote Revelations of Divine Love — the first book in English known to be written by a woman. She speaks of God's love, Christ as mother and the hope that 'all shall be well'.

people.name: Catherine of Siena
people.summary: Dominican tertiary and mystic who, though largely unschooled, dictated The Dialogue and hundreds of letters to popes and rulers. She urged Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome and worked for church unity during the Western Schism. Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970.

people.name: Jan Hus
people.summary: Czech preacher at Prague's Bethlehem Chapel and rector of the university, influenced by Wycliffe. He criticised indulgences and clerical corruption and defined the church as the community of the predestined. Summoned to Constance under safe-conduct, he was burned on 6 July 1415, sparking the Hussite movement.
keyIdeas: Christ, not the pope, as head of the church
Communion in both kinds (taken up by followers)

people.name: Afonso I of Kongo (Mvemba a Nzinga)
people.summary: King of Kongo from 1509 who made Catholicism the religion of his court, studied the Scriptures and canon law, and sent his son Henrique to Lisbon and Rome to become a bishop. His letters to King João III protested Portuguese slave-trading that was depopulating his kingdom.

people.name: Desiderius Erasmus
people.summary: Dutch humanist, the most famous scholar of his day, whose Greek New Testament (1516) and editions of the Fathers fuelled the call 'back to the sources'. He satirised clerical abuses in The Praise of Folly but stayed Catholic, debating Luther on free will (1524–25).
keyIdeas: Return to biblical and patristic sources

people.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
people.summary: Spanish colonist and encomendero who, convicted by preaching on Sirach 34, freed his Indigenous labourers, became a Dominican and spent fifty years denouncing the conquest's cruelties. Bishop of Chiapas, author of A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, he argued at Valladolid (1550) for Indigenous rights; he early proposed African slaves as substitutes, which he later repented.
keyIdeas: Indigenous peoples as rational and free

people.name: Huldrych Zwingli
people.summary: Swiss humanist priest who, from 1519 at Zürich's Grossmünster, preached through the Bible and led the city's Reformation: abolishing the Mass, images and fasting rules. He taught a symbolic, memorial view of the Lord's Supper, broke with Luther at Marburg and died in battle at Kappel.

people.name: Martin Luther
people.summary: Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor whose protest against indulgences (1517) became the Protestant Reformation. He taught justification by grace through faith alone, the authority of Scripture over popes and councils and the priesthood of all believers, and translated the Bible into German. Excommunicated in 1521, he married Katharina von Bora and shaped Lutheran worship with hymns and catechisms; his late anti-Jewish writings are widely repudiated today.

people.name: Thomas Müntzer
people.summary: An early follower of Luther who turned against him, preaching direct revelation of the Spirit, apocalyptic judgement on the ungodly and the rights of the common people. He led peasant forces at Frankenhausen and was executed in 1525.

people.name: Thomas Cranmer
people.summary: Archbishop of Canterbury under Henry VIII and Edward VI who annulled Henry's marriage and shaped the English Reformation. His Books of Common Prayer (1549, 1552) and Forty-two Articles defined Anglican worship and doctrine. Under Mary I he recanted, then withdrew his recantations and was burned at Oxford.

people.name: Balthasar Hubmaier
people.summary: A doctor of theology and former Catholic preacher who became the most learned early Anabaptist, writing on believers' baptism and religious freedom (On Heretics and Those Who Burn Them). Unlike the Swiss Brethren he accepted the magistrate's sword. He was burned in Vienna in 1528.

people.name: Ignatius of Loyola
people.summary: Basque soldier converted while recovering from wounds (1521), who devised the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Society of Jesus (1540). The Jesuits became the leading force of Catholic renewal in education and global mission.

people.name: Menno Simons
people.summary: Frisian priest who, disturbed by the Münster debacle in which his brother died, joined the peaceful Anabaptists in 1536. As itinerant elder with a price on his head he gathered scattered congregations; his followers became known as Mennonites.

people.name: Philip Melanchthon
people.summary: Humanist Greek professor at Wittenberg, Luther's closest colleague, who wrote the first Protestant systematic theology (Loci communes, 1521) and the Augsburg Confession (1530). Called 'Teacher of Germany' for his educational reforms; his irenic stance provoked later Lutheran disputes.

people.name: Conrad Grebel
people.summary: Son of a Zürich patrician, a humanist student of Zwingli who broke with him over infant baptism and state control of reform. On 21 January 1525 he baptised George Blaurock, beginning the Anabaptist movement; he died of plague the following year.

people.name: Heinrich Bullinger
people.summary: Zwingli's successor at Zürich for 44 years, the most widely read Reformed theologian of the 16th century. He wrote the Second Helvetic Confession (1566), the Decades of sermons and the Consensus Tigurinus with Calvin (1549); he developed covenant theology.
keyIdeas: Preaching of the Word is the Word of God

people.name: Francis Xavier
people.summary: Navarrese co-founder of the Jesuits who sailed to Goa in 1542 and preached among the Parava pearl-fishers of south India, in the Moluccas and from 1549 in Japan. He died on Shangchuan Island off China awaiting entry. His tomb in Goa remains a pilgrimage site.

people.name: John Calvin
people.summary: French humanist lawyer converted to evangelical faith, who led the Reformation in Geneva from 1541. His Institutes of the Christian Religion and biblical commentaries systematised Reformed theology: God's sovereignty, union with Christ, double grace of justification and sanctification, spiritual real presence and predestination. Geneva trained pastors for France, Scotland and beyond; his role in Servetus's execution remains a lasting stain.

people.name: Teresa of Ávila
people.summary: Spanish Carmelite nun of converso descent who founded the reformed Discalced Carmelites. Her Life, The Way of Perfection and The Interior Castle map the soul's journey through prayer to union with God. In 1970 she became the first woman declared a Doctor of the Church.
keyIdeas: Mental prayer as friendship with God

people.name: Theodore Beza
people.summary: French humanist who succeeded Calvin as leader of Geneva's church and academy. He edited the Greek New Testament, defended Huguenot resistance after St Bartholomew's Day, and systematised predestination in a more scholastic, supralapsarian direction.

people.name: John of the Cross
people.summary: Spanish Carmelite friar who joined Teresa's reform and was imprisoned by his own order. His poems and commentaries — The Dark Night of the Soul, Ascent of Mount Carmel, Spiritual Canticle — describe purgation and union with God through faith beyond images.

people.name: Matteo Ricci
people.summary: Italian Jesuit who entered China in 1582 and lived in Beijing from 1601. Adopting the dress and learning of Confucian scholars, he wrote The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, made a famous world map and translated Euclid with Xu Guangqi. His accommodation of ancestral rites was later condemned.

people.name: Jacobus Arminius
people.summary: Dutch Reformed pastor and Leiden professor, trained under Beza, who came to teach that God elects those he foresees will believe, that grace may be resisted and that Christ died for all. His followers' Remonstrance was condemned at Dort; Arminian theology later shaped Methodism and much of evangelicalism.

people.name: Cyril Lucaris
people.summary: Cretan-born patriarch of Alexandria and then Constantinople, who sought Protestant allies against Jesuit influence and published a Confession with Calvinist doctrines (1629). Repeatedly deposed and restored by Ottoman politics, he was strangled in 1638; Orthodox synods condemned the Confession.

people.name: Hugo Grotius
people.summary: Dutch prodigy and Remonstrant sympathiser imprisoned after Dort, who escaped in a book chest. His On the Law of War and Peace founded international law, and his defence of the satisfaction of Christ developed the 'governmental' theory of the atonement.

people.name: Cornelius Jansen
people.summary: Flemish theologian and bishop of Ypres whose posthumous Augustinus (1640) argued for Augustine's strong doctrine of efficacious grace against Jesuit theologians. Five propositions attributed to it were condemned in 1653; 'Jansenism' became a rigorist movement centred on Port-Royal.

people.name: Rose of Lima
people.summary: Isabel Flores de Oliva, a Dominican tertiary in Lima known for severe penances, care for the poor and sick, and mystical prayer. Canonised in 1671, she was the first saint born in the Americas and is patroness of Latin America.

people.name: Richard Baxter
people.summary: Puritan pastor whose ministry transformed Kidderminster through catechising households. A moderate who sought unity, he was ejected in 1662 and later imprisoned. The Reformed Pastor and The Saints' Everlasting Rest made him one of the most widely read devotional writers.

people.name: John Owen
people.summary: Leading Puritan theologian, chaplain to Cromwell and vice-chancellor of Oxford, later an Independent pastor in London. His The Death of Death in the Death of Christ defends particular redemption; other works treat communion with the Trinity, mortification of sin and the Holy Spirit.

people.name: Blaise Pascal
people.summary: French mathematician and physicist who, after a night of fire in November 1654 recorded in his Memorial, devoted himself to faith in association with Port-Royal. His Provincial Letters satirised Jesuit casuistry, and his unfinished apology, the Pensées, includes the famous 'wager'.

people.name: George Fox
people.summary: English weaver's son and seeker who in 1647 heard 'There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition'. He founded the Religious Society of Friends, preaching the Inward Light, rejecting steeple-houses, tithes and oaths; he was imprisoned repeatedly and travelled to America and the Netherlands.
keyIdeas: No professional clergy or outward sacraments

people.name: Philipp Jakob Spener
people.summary: Lutheran pastor at Frankfurt, Dresden and Berlin, often called the father of Pietism. His Pia Desideria (1675) proposed Bible study groups, lay priesthood, practical faith and heartfelt preaching to renew a church he saw as formal and quarrelsome.

people.name: Jacob Ammann
people.summary: Swiss Brethren elder in Alsace whose call for strict social shunning, twice-yearly communion with foot-washing and plain dress led to the division of 1693. His followers, the Amish, later settled in Pennsylvania and spread across North America.

people.name: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg
people.summary: German Pietist from Halle sent by the Danish king to Tranquebar in 1706, the first Protestant missionary in India. He mastered Tamil, translated the New Testament (1714), founded schools and a printing press, and wrote sympathetic studies of South Indian religion.

people.name: Kimpa Vita (Dona Beatriz)
people.summary: A Kongolese noblewoman who in 1704 announced she had died and been possessed by St Anthony, preaching that Christ and Mary were Kongolese and calling for the kingdom's reunification. Her Antonian movement drew thousands to the ruined capital; condemned by Capuchins, she was burned in 1706.
keyIdeas: Political and spiritual renewal of Kongo

people.name: Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf
people.summary: Saxon nobleman raised in Halle Pietism who sheltered Moravian refugees at Herrnhut and became their bishop. His 'religion of the heart' centred on the wounds of the Lamb; he launched worldwide missions and founded settlements such as Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.
keyIdeas: Heart religion centred on Christ's wounds

people.name: Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin
people.summary: A Nahua convert to whom, according to the Guadalupe tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared at Tepeyac in December 1531. Historical documentation is debated, but he was canonised in 2002 as the first Indigenous saint of the Americas.

people.name: Jonathan Edwards
people.summary: New England Congregationalist pastor whose Northampton revival (1734–35) and writings — A Faithful Narrative, Religious Affections, Freedom of the Will — made him the theologian of the Great Awakening. Dismissed by his church in 1750, he served as missionary to the Mohicans at Stockbridge and died as president of Princeton. He also enslaved people, a fact now prominently discussed.
keyIdeas: Religious affections as mark of true religion

people.name: John Wesley
people.summary: Anglican priest whose heart was 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate in 1738. Riding some 250,000 miles, he preached in the open air and organised converts into societies, classes and bands, creating Methodism. He taught universal grace, assurance and Christian perfection (entire sanctification) and opposed slavery.

people.name: Charles Wesley
people.summary: John's younger brother, converted days before him in May 1738, who wrote some 6,000 hymns including 'Hark! the Herald Angels Sing' and 'And Can It Be'. His hymns taught Methodist theology to ordinary believers; he remained firmly loyal to the Church of England.

people.name: George Whitefield
people.summary: Anglican evangelist whose dramatic open-air preaching drew crowds of tens of thousands in Britain and the American colonies, uniting the First Great Awakening. A Calvinist Methodist, he differed from Wesley on predestination. He also defended slavery in Georgia, a stain on his legacy.

people.name: Paisius Velichkovsky
people.summary: Ukrainian monk who lived on Mount Athos and later led large communities in Moldavia at Dragomirna and Neamț. His Slavonic translation of the Philokalia (1793) spread hesychast prayer and spiritual eldership through Russia, inspiring the startsy of Optina.

people.name: Yi Seung-hun (Peter)
people.summary: A Korean Confucian scholar who, after studying Catholic books, was baptised in Beijing in 1784 as Peter and returned to found a lay-led church in Korea. He was beheaded in the Sinyu persecution of 1801.

people.name: William Wilberforce
people.summary: Member of Parliament for Yorkshire whose evangelical conversion (1785) led him, with the Clapham Sect, Quakers and Black abolitionists, to campaign for abolition of the slave trade, achieved in 1807. He died days after the Slavery Abolition Act passed in 1833.

people.name: William Carey
people.summary: English shoemaker and Baptist pastor whose Enquiry (1792) helped found the Baptist Missionary Society. In India from 1793, he and colleagues at Serampore translated the Bible into dozens of languages, founded Serampore College and campaigned against sati. He is often called 'the father of modern missions'.

people.name: Friedrich Schleiermacher
people.summary: Prussian Reformed theologian raised among the Moravians, often called the father of modern liberal theology. His Speeches on Religion and The Christian Faith ground doctrine in the 'feeling of absolute dependence' on God and reinterpret it in relation to Christ's God-consciousness.
keyIdeas: Religion as feeling of absolute dependence
Doctrine as expression of Christian experience

people.name: William Miller
people.summary: Baptist farmer-preacher who calculated from Daniel 8:14 that Christ would return around 1843–44. His movement drew perhaps 50,000–100,000 followers; after the Great Disappointment of 22 October 1844 he acknowledged his error but kept hoping for an imminent return.

people.name: Robert Morrison
people.summary: London Missionary Society missionary, the first Protestant missionary in China (1807). Working under East India Company restrictions, he translated the Bible into Chinese with William Milne and compiled a monumental Chinese–English dictionary.

people.name: Charles Grandison Finney
people.summary: Lawyer turned revivalist in upstate New York's 'burned-over district' who introduced 'new measures' such as the anxious bench and protracted meetings, teaching that revival is the right use of means. As president of Oberlin College he promoted abolition, coeducation and perfectionism.
keyIdeas: Social reform as fruit of conversion

people.name: Charles Hodge
people.summary: Professor at Princeton Theological Seminary for over fifty years, whose Systematic Theology championed Reformed confessional orthodoxy and the inspiration of Scripture. He criticised Darwinism as atheistic where it excluded design, and contributed to the Princeton doctrine of inerrancy.

people.name: John Nelson Darby
people.summary: Anglo-Irish former Anglican priest, a founder of the Plymouth Brethren. He developed dispensationalism, distinguishing Israel from the church and teaching a secret pre-tribulation rapture; his ideas spread through Bible conferences and later the Scofield Reference Bible.

people.name: John McLeod Campbell
people.summary: Church of Scotland minister deposed in 1831 for teaching that Christ died for all and that believers may have assurance. His The Nature of the Atonement (1856) presents Christ's 'vicarious repentance' — a perfect confession of the Father's judgement on sin — and influenced the Torrances.

people.name: Joseph Smith
people.summary: Founder of the Latter Day Saint movement, who reported visions of God the Father and Jesus (1820) and an angel guiding him to golden plates he published as the Book of Mormon (1830). He led his followers from New York to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo, introduced temple rites and plural marriage, and was killed by a mob at Carthage jail. His movement stands outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
keyIdeas: Restoration of the church through new revelation

people.name: Phoebe Palmer
people.summary: Methodist laywoman whose Tuesday Meeting for the Promotion of Holiness in New York and book The Way of Holiness taught an 'altar theology' of instantaneous entire sanctification by consecration and faith. She preached widely and defended women's ministry in Promise of the Father.

people.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
people.summary: A Yoruba boy enslaved in 1821 and freed by the Royal Navy, educated in Freetown, who became the first African Anglican bishop (1864) in charge of the Niger Mission. He translated the Bible into Yoruba and compiled grammars of several languages; European missionaries' undermining of his authority before his death became a turning point for African church independence.

people.name: Andrew Kim Taegon
people.summary: The first Korean-born Catholic priest, trained in Macau and ordained in Shanghai in 1845. Arrested while arranging missionary entry by sea, he was beheaded at Saenamteo near Seoul aged 25; he is the patron of Korean clergy, canonised with 102 companions in 1984.

people.name: Ellen G. White
people.summary: A Millerite who reported some 2,000 visions after 1844 and co-founded the Seventh-day Adventist Church (1863). Adventists regard her as a messenger with the gift of prophecy, subordinate to Scripture; her writings shaped Sabbath observance, health reform and education. Critics question her claims and borrowings from other authors.
keyIdeas: Great controversy between Christ and Satan

people.name: James Hudson Taylor
people.summary: Yorkshire-born missionary to China who founded the China Inland Mission (1865), sending interdenominational missionaries — including many single women — into all of China's interior provinces. He adopted Chinese dress and pioneered the 'faith mission' model of trusting God for support.

people.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
people.summary: Baptist pastor of London's Metropolitan Tabernacle, the most popular preacher of Victorian England, whose sermons were printed weekly and sold worldwide. A Calvinist evangelist, he founded a college and orphanage and left the Baptist Union during the Downgrade controversy (1887).

people.name: Cyrus I. Scofield
people.summary: Lawyer and Congregational minister in Dallas whose Scofield Reference Bible (1909, rev. 1917) set dispensational premillennialism in its notes. It became the most influential study Bible among American fundamentalists.

people.name: Charles Taze Russell
people.summary: Pittsburgh businessman influenced by Adventist teachers who founded the Bible Student movement and Zion's Watch Tower (1879). He rejected the Trinity and eternal torment and predicted the end of the Gentile Times in 1914. Jehovah's Witnesses, organised after him, stand outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
keyIdeas: Rejection of the Trinity and hellfire

people.name: Pandita Ramabai
people.summary: A Brahmin Sanskrit scholar and widow who embraced Christianity in England (1883) and founded the Mukti Mission for widows and abandoned girls near Pune. A pioneer of women's rights in India, she translated the Bible into Marathi from the original languages; her mission saw a notable revival in 1905.

people.name: William Wade Harris
people.summary: A Liberian Grebo teacher and former Methodist and Episcopal worker who, after a vision in prison in 1910, walked along the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast (1913–15) as a prophet in white robes. He baptised perhaps 120,000 people, the largest mass movement in West African history, before French expulsion.

people.name: Walter Rauschenbusch
people.summary: German-American Baptist pastor in New York's 'Hell's Kitchen' and Rochester seminary professor, the leading voice of the Social Gospel. Christianity and the Social Crisis and A Theology for the Social Gospel called churches to work for the Kingdom of God in economic and social structures.
keyIdeas: Kingdom of God as social transformation

people.name: Uchimura Kanzō
people.summary: Japanese Christian writer converted at Sapporo Agricultural College, who refused to bow before the Imperial Rescript on Education (1891). He founded the Mukyōkai ('Non-Church') movement of Bible study without clergy or sacraments, seeking a Christianity rooted in Japanese soil.

people.name: Tikhon of Moscow
people.summary: Bishop for North America (1898–1907), where he helped organise Orthodoxy among immigrants, then elected Patriarch of Moscow in 1917. He anathematised Bolshevik violence, was imprisoned and pressured by the Soviet state and died in 1925; he was canonised in 1989.

people.name: Isaiah Shembe
people.summary: Zulu healer and prophet who founded the amaNazaretha (Nazareth Baptist Church) in 1910, with a holy city at Ekuphakameni and pilgrimage to the mountain Nhlangakazi. His hymns blend biblical faith with Zulu culture; his followers venerate him as a prophet sent to Africa.

people.name: William J. Seymour
people.summary: Son of formerly enslaved parents in Louisiana, a Holiness preacher blind in one eye who accepted Parham's teaching on tongues. As pastor of the Apostolic Faith Mission on Azusa Street from 1906 he led the interracial revival that launched worldwide Pentecostalism; he later emphasised love and unity over tongues as the evidence of the Spirit.
keyIdeas: Love as evidence of the Spirit

people.name: Charles Fox Parham
people.summary: Holiness preacher whose Bethel Bible School in Topeka saw Agnes Ozman speak in tongues on 1 January 1901. He formulated the doctrine that tongues are the initial evidence of Spirit baptism and taught Seymour in Houston, but rejected Azusa's interracial worship and later supported segregation; a 1907 scandal diminished his influence.

people.name: V. S. Azariah
people.summary: Tamil evangelist who founded the Indian Missionary Society and became the first Indian Anglican bishop (Dornakal, 1912). He led mass movements among Dalit communities in Telugu country, pleaded at Edinburgh 1910 for true friendship between missionaries and Indian Christians, and worked for the union that produced the Church of South India.

people.name: Evan Roberts
people.summary: Former coal miner and ministerial student whose meetings in Loughor in late 1904 sparked the Welsh Revival. His four-point call — confess sin, remove doubtful things, obey the Spirit promptly, confess Christ publicly — spread across Wales; after a breakdown he withdrew into private prayer for decades.

people.name: Gustaf Aulén
people.summary: Swedish Lutheran theologian of the Lund school and bishop of Strängnäs, whose Christus Victor (1931) argued that the 'classic' patristic and Lutheran view of the atonement is Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil, distinct from Latin satisfaction and liberal moral-influence theories.

people.name: John XXIII
people.summary: Angelo Roncalli, papal diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and France and patriarch of Venice, elected pope in 1958 as a caretaker. He surprised the world by calling the Second Vatican Council for aggiornamento and wrote Pacem in Terris on peace and human rights; he was canonised in 2014.

people.name: Rudolf Bultmann
people.summary: Marburg New Testament scholar who pioneered form criticism and called for 'demythologising' the New Testament — interpreting its mythic world-picture existentially as a call to authentic faith. Influential and contested, he was also a member of the Confessing Church.

people.name: Karl Barth
people.summary: Swiss Reformed pastor whose commentary on Romans (1919) broke with liberal theology, insisting on God's sovereign self-revelation in Jesus Christ. Principal author of the Barmen Declaration, expelled from Germany in 1935, he wrote the vast Church Dogmatics, recasting election as God's choice of humanity in Christ.
keyIdeas: Word of God in threefold form

people.name: Simon Kimbangu
people.summary: A Baptist catechist in the Belgian Congo whose healing ministry from April 1921 drew multitudes to Nkamba. Arrested by colonial authorities within months, he spent thirty years in prison in Lubumbashi, where he died. The Kimbanguist Church that bears his name became one of Africa's largest independent churches.

people.name: Toyohiko Kagawa
people.summary: Japanese Christian who lived in the Shinkawa slum of Kobe from 1909, founding labour and agricultural unions and cooperatives. A prolific writer and evangelist of the Kingdom of God movement, he was imprisoned for pacifism and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.
keyIdeas: Love in action among the poor

people.name: Sadhu Sundar Singh
people.summary: A Sikh youth who, after burning a Bible, reported a vision of Christ in 1904 and became a wandering sadhu preaching Christ in Indian dress. He travelled through India, Tibet and the West; he disappeared in the Himalayas in 1929. He exemplified an Indian form of Christian devotion.
keyIdeas: Christ in Indian form ('water of life in an Indian cup')

people.name: Pius IX
people.summary: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, pope for 31 years (1846–78), the longest pontificate. Initially liberal, he turned against liberalism after 1848, issued the Syllabus of Errors (1864), defined the Immaculate Conception (1854) and convened Vatican I, which defined papal infallibility, as the Papal States were lost. The Mortara affair darkened his reputation.

people.name: Pius XII
people.summary: Eugenio Pacelli, nuncio in Germany and Vatican secretary of state, pope from 1939 to 1958. He guided the church through World War II — his public reticence about the Holocaust remains intensely debated alongside documented rescue efforts — encouraged biblical scholarship (Divino Afflante Spiritu, 1943) and defined the Assumption (1950).

people.name: C. S. Lewis
people.summary: Belfast-born Oxford and Cambridge literary scholar who returned to Christian faith in 1931. His wartime broadcasts became Mere Christianity; The Screwtape Letters, The Chronicles of Narnia and The Great Divorce made him the most popular Christian writer of the 20th century across traditions.

people.name: John Sung (Song Shangjie)
people.summary: Son of a Methodist pastor in Fujian who earned a chemistry PhD in the United States before a dramatic conversion in 1927. Returning to China, he became the most powerful revivalist in Chinese history, holding campaigns across China and Southeast Asia with fiery preaching, healing prayer and evangelistic bands.

people.name: Watchman Nee (Ni Tuosheng)
people.summary: Chinese Christian leader influenced by the Brethren, who founded the 'Little Flock' (local churches) movement and wrote The Normal Christian Life and The Spiritual Man. Arrested in 1952, he died in a labour camp after twenty years; his teaching shaped Chinese house churches worldwide.

people.name: Karl Rahner
people.summary: German Jesuit, perhaps the most influential Catholic theologian of the 20th century and a peritus at Vatican II. His transcendental theology described humans as oriented toward holy mystery; his ideas of the 'supernatural existential' and 'anonymous Christians' reshaped Catholic thought on grace and other religions. 'Rahner's Rule' identifies the economic and immanent Trinity.

people.name: Joseph Ayo Babalola
people.summary: A Yoruba steamroller driver who heard a divine call in 1928 and led the Ilesa healing revival of 1930. He became the spiritual leader of the Christ Apostolic Church, one of Nigeria's largest Aladura churches, emphasising prayer, fasting and healing without medicine.

people.name: Hans Urs von Balthasar
people.summary: Swiss Catholic theologian whose trilogy — The Glory of the Lord, Theo-Drama and Theo-Logic — begins theology from divine beauty. Influenced by Adrienne von Speyr, he wrote on Christ's descent into hell and a 'hope' that all may be saved; named cardinal shortly before his death.
keyIdeas: Dare we hope that all be saved

people.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
people.summary: German Lutheran theologian of the Confessing Church who led an underground seminary at Finkenwalde, wrote Discipleship (critiquing 'cheap grace') and Life Together, and joined the conspiracy against Hitler. Imprisoned in 1943, he was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945; his prison letters speculated on 'religionless Christianity'.

people.name: Teresa of Calcutta
people.summary: Albanian-born Loreto sister who in 1950 founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta to serve 'the poorest of the poor', dying and abandoned. She won the Nobel Peace Prize (1979) and was canonised in 2016; critics questioned care standards in her homes, and her letters revealed decades of spiritual darkness.

people.name: Thomas F. Torrance
people.summary: Scottish theologian born to missionary parents in China, a student of Barth and editor of the Church Dogmatics in English. At Edinburgh he developed a Trinitarian, incarnational theology drawing on Athanasius and Cyril, dialogued with science, and led Reformed–Orthodox agreement on the Trinity (1991).

people.name: Óscar Romero
people.summary: A conservative cleric appointed archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, who was transformed by the murder of his friend the Jesuit Rutilio Grande into a fearless voice for the poor and victims of state violence. He was shot at the altar on 24 March 1980 and canonised in 2018.

people.name: Kenneth E. Hagin
people.summary: Texas-born Pentecostal preacher, healed as a teenager, who became the leading teacher of the Word of Faith movement through Rhema Bible Training Center in Tulsa. He taught positive confession of God's promises for healing and prosperity; critics, including Pentecostals, faulted its theology.

people.name: Billy Graham
people.summary: Southern Baptist evangelist who preached in person to an estimated 215 million people in over 185 countries. He helped forge post-war 'neo-evangelicalism', founded Christianity Today and convened the Lausanne Congress (1974); he desegregated his crusades in the 1950s and advised many presidents.

people.name: Oral Roberts
people.summary: Pentecostal Holiness evangelist whose tent healing crusades and pioneering television broadcasts brought Pentecostalism into American living rooms. He founded Oral Roberts University (1963), joined the United Methodist Church (1968) and popularised 'seed-faith' giving.

people.name: John Paul II
people.summary: Karol Wojtyła, archbishop of Kraków, elected the first non-Italian pope in 455 years in 1978. His pilgrimages to over 120 countries, support for Solidarity in Poland, theology of the body and outreach to Jews and other Christians defined his 27-year pontificate; critics fault his handling of clerical abuse. He was canonised in 2014.

people.name: John Stott
people.summary: Rector of All Souls, Langham Place, London, a leading statesman of global evangelicalism. Chief architect of the Lausanne Covenant (1974), author of The Cross of Christ and Basic Christianity, he advocated integrating evangelism and social responsibility and, tentatively, conditional immortality.

place.name: All Souls Church, Langham Place, London

people.name: James B. Torrance
people.summary: Scottish theologian at Aberdeen, younger brother of Thomas Torrance, who criticised 'federal' (contract) Calvinism and stressed God's unconditional covenant of grace. His Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace presents worship as participation through the Spirit in the Son's communion with the Father.
keyIdeas: Worship as participation in Christ's priesthood

people.name: René Girard
people.summary: French-American scholar whose mimetic theory argues that human desire is imitative, leading to rivalry resolved by the collective killing of a scapegoat. He read the Gospels as exposing the scapegoat mechanism through the innocent victim Jesus, influencing nonviolent theories of the atonement.

people.name: J. I. Packer
people.summary: English Anglican Reformed theologian, later professor at Regent College, Vancouver, whose Knowing God became a modern classic. He defended biblical inerrancy, penal substitution ('What Did the Cross Achieve?') and Puritan spirituality, and supported Evangelicals and Catholics Together.

people.name: Jürgen Moltmann
people.summary: German Reformed theologian, converted as a prisoner of war, whose Theology of Hope (1964) and The Crucified God (1972) placed eschatology and the suffering of God at the centre of theology. He influenced liberation and political theologies and ecological theology.

people.name: Gustavo Gutiérrez
people.summary: Peruvian priest, later Dominican, whose A Theology of Liberation (1971) named the movement. He argued that theology is critical reflection on praxis in light of God's word, that salvation includes liberation from oppression, and that God shows a preferential option for the poor. The Vatican critiqued aspects of liberation theology in 1984, but Gutiérrez remained in good standing.

people.name: Hal Lindsey
people.summary: American evangelist whose The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), a popular dispensationalist reading of current events as fulfilling prophecy, became the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s. His predictions about the generation after 1948 did not come to pass.

people.name: C. Peter Wagner
people.summary: Former missionary in Bolivia and Fuller Seminary professor of church growth who coined the 'Third Wave' of the Spirit, taught with John Wimber, and later led the New Apostolic Reformation emphasising modern apostles, prophets and strategic spiritual warfare. His later teachings drew widespread criticism.

people.name: Desmond Tutu
people.summary: Anglican archbishop of Cape Town and Nobel Peace laureate (1984) who led nonviolent church opposition to apartheid. As chair of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, he championed restorative justice and ubuntu theology; he later advocated LGBT inclusion.

people.name: John Wimber
people.summary: Former rock musician who became leader of the Association of Vineyard Churches. His 'power evangelism' and 'doin' the stuff' approach taught ordinary believers to pray for healing; his Fuller Seminary course with Peter Wagner popularised the Third Wave. Vineyard worship shaped contemporary music.

people.name: Pope Francis
people.summary: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Jesuit archbishop of Buenos Aires, elected in 2013 as the first pope from the Americas. His pontificate stressed mercy, care for the poor and migrants, creation (Laudato si') and synodality, provoking both enthusiasm and traditionalist opposition. He died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025.

people.name: David Yonggi Cho
people.summary: Korean Pentecostal pastor who, after healing from tuberculosis, founded Yoido Full Gospel Church in 1958, growing it through home cell groups into the world's largest congregation. He taught a 'threefold blessing' of salvation, health and prosperity; in 2014 he was convicted of embezzlement involving church funds.

people.name: Edward Fudge
people.summary: American Church of Christ theologian and lawyer whose The Fire That Consumes (1982) made the evangelical case for conditional immortality — that the unsaved are finally destroyed rather than tormented eternally. It persuaded many evangelicals and provoked extended debate.

people.name: Kwame Bediako
people.summary: Ghanaian Presbyterian theologian who founded the Akrofi-Christaller Institute at Akropong. In Theology and Identity and Christianity in Africa he argued that African Christianity is a 'non-Western religion' continuous with pre-Christian African religious heritage, like the early church's engagement with Hellenism.

people.name: John Piper
people.summary: Long-time pastor of Bethlehem Baptist Church in Minneapolis and founder of Desiring God, whose Desiring God (1986) propounded 'Christian hedonism'. A leading voice of the 'young, restless, Reformed' movement, he defends Calvinist soteriology, penal substitution and complementarianism.

people.name: N. T. Wright
people.summary: English New Testament scholar and former bishop of Durham, a leading figure in the 'New Perspective on Paul'. His Christian Origins and the Question of God series argues for the historical Jesus as Israel's Messiah and for bodily resurrection, and he reframes justification around covenant membership.
keyIdeas: Jesus and the story of Israel

people.name: C. Baxter Kruger
people.summary: American theologian and director of Perichoresis, whose books such as The Great Dance and The Shack Revisited popularise a 'Trinitarian theology' emphasising humanity's adoption into the life of the Trinity through Christ, drawing on Athanasius and the Torrances. Critics see in it a tendency toward universalism.

people.name: François du Toit
people.summary: South African teacher of the 'Mirror Word' movement and author of The Mirror Bible, a paraphrase of the New Testament emphasising humanity's union with Christ through his death and resurrection. His teaching is often associated with 'finished work' and universalist-leaning views that many evangelicals reject.
keyIdeas: Union with Christ of all humanity
Mirror reflection of identity in Christ

people.name: Rob Bell
people.summary: Founding pastor of Mars Hill Bible Church in Michigan, whose Love Wins (2011) questioned traditional teaching on eternal punishment and suggested God's love may ultimately reconcile all. The book provoked fierce controversy among evangelicals; he left the church in 2012.
